passages.context: Bivin's reply, read in full in the retrieved capture. It observes that none of the perpetuators of the claim offers any evidence and that none cites a biblical or rabbinic source; sets out the lexical facts about soudarion as a Latin loanword and its three other New Testament occurrences; asks whether napkins were used at all in first-century Israel and notes that no early rabbinic source discusses how the hands were dried after washing; and concludes with four conditions the claim would require, including that the Greek word mean having been folded rather than having been wrapped up, together with the conjecture that the story was triggered by the archaic King James translation napkin.
passages.notes: Bivin is a specialist in the Jewish background of the Gospels, which makes this the earliest expert refutation located. His lexical claims were not taken on trust: the consuming publication checks soudarion and entylisso independently against a registered lexicon.

work.author: David Bivin, answering a reader, for JerusalemPerspective.com
work.description: The earliest dated appearance located of the modern claim that a folded napkin was a Jewish master-and-servant signal meaning I am coming back. The page prints a reader's question quoting the claim in its now-standard wording and David Bivin's reply, which observes that no version of the claim cites a biblical or rabbinic source and conjectures that the whole story was invented out of the archaic King James word napkin. Registered as dated evidence of the claim's circulation and of its earliest recorded refutation.
work.title: Christ's Linen Napkin (John 20:7): Is it significant that the napkin that had been around Jesus' head when he was buried was found in the empty tomb folded?
